channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You prefer a sure gain, even when a gamble pays more.
item.description: The pseudocertainty effect leads people to choose an outcome perceived as certain over a probabilistic one, even when the latter is mathematically superior.

item.title: You complete tasks in the time you allocate, regardless of complexity.
item.description: Parkinson's Law states that work expands to fill the time available for its completion.

item.title: A single new possession creates a spiral of forced consumption.
item.description: The Diderot effect describes how a new item that deviates from your existing lifestyle leads to a cycle of purchasing to regain consistency.

item.title: You consistently overestimate your ability to handle immediate temptation.
item.description: The restraint bias is a pattern where individuals overestimate their self-control and consequently put themselves in situations they cannot manage.

item.title: You over-allocate resources to eliminate a minor, symbolic risk.
item.description: The zero-risk bias leads people to prefer the complete elimination of a small risk over a greater total reduction in risk elsewhere.

item.title: You judge past decisions by their results, not their logic.
item.description: The outcome bias causes people to retrospectively evaluate a decision as poor if the result was unfavorable, even if the decision-making process was sound.

item.title: Your expectations of others physically alter their actual performance.
item.description: The Pygmalion effect demonstrates that higher expectations from an authority figure lead to an improvement in an individual's performance.

item.title: You believe you understand others better than they understand you.
item.description: The illusion of asymmetric insight is the tendency for people to believe that they know others better than others know them, and that they are more knowable to others than others are to them.

item.title: You make decisions based on the most easily recalled examples.
item.description: The availability heuristic leads you to judge the probability of events based on how easily specific instances come to mind.

item.title: You like things more simply because you have seen them.
item.description: The mere exposure effect is the tendency to develop a preference for stimuli merely because you are familiar with them.

item.title: You think your future self will share your current tastes.
item.description: The projection bias is your systematic failure to predict how your future preferences will change based on your current state.

item.title: Rewarding a task you enjoy kills your intrinsic motivation.
item.description: The foundational 1973 study by Lepper, Greene, and Nisbett demonstrated the effect using art and drawing activities, not puzzles.

item.title: You assume generic descriptions apply specifically to you.
item.description: The phenomenon is known as the Forer effect or the fallacy of personal validation, while the term 'Barnum effect' was later coined by Paul E. Meehl in 1956.

item.title: You stop remembering facts you know are stored digitally.
item.description: The Google effect shows that you are less likely to remember information if you believe it is easily accessible online.

item.title: You remember the message but forget the unreliable source.
item.description: The sleeper effect occurs when the persuasiveness of a message increases over time as you decouple it from its source.

item.title: You feel more successful when your group achieves a win.
item.description: Basking in reflected glory is the psychological attempt to maintain self-esteem by aligning yourself with successful others.

item.title: You take personal credit for wins but blame external luck.
item.description: The self-serving bias is the tendency to attribute success to your internal character and failure to your environment.

item.title: You feel more regret for things that nearly happened.
item.description: Counterfactual thinking causes stronger emotional reactions to 'near misses' than to outcomes that were never possible.

item.title: You value the things you own more than identical objects.
item.description: The mere ownership effect demonstrates that merely possessing an item increases its perceived value significantly.

item.title: You believe past events were more predictable than they were.
item.description: Hindsight bias causes you to view historical outcomes as inevitable despite the inherent uncertainty of the time.

item.title: You find statements more true if they simply rhyme.
item.description: Rhyming statements are processed as more accurate and truthful than non-rhyming statements.

item.title: You consistently believe you are more capable than you are.
item.description: While researchers have found that individuals often rate themselves as above average in various domains, the 1977 study by Lichtenstein and Fischhoff focuses on the calibration of probability assessments rather than relative self-evaluation.

item.title: You believe your future work will be faster today.
item.description: People consistently underestimate how long tasks take, even with past evidence.

item.title: Your brain weighs bad experiences more than good ones.
item.description: Negative stimuli elicit stronger physiological and psychological responses than positive stimuli.

item.title: You judge how likely something is by your memory.
item.description: The ease with which examples come to mind determines your probability assessment.

item.title: You assume a person's appearance reveals their inner character.
item.description: A single positive trait leads people to assume other unrelated positive qualities exist.

item.title: You only clearly remember the beginning and the end.
item.description: Information presented at the start and conclusion of a list is significantly better retained.

item.title: You prioritize immediate satisfaction over long-term gain every time.
item.description: People often choose a smaller, immediate reward over a larger, delayed one, but their preferences frequently reverse in favor of the larger, later reward when both options are set in the future.

item.title: Your opinion shifts to match the perceived group consensus.
item.description: A 1951 study showed that participants would give a clearly incorrect answer just to align with the rest of the group.

item.title: You selectively interpret facts to protect your existing worldview.
item.description: A 1979 study found that participants shown balanced evidence on capital punishment were convinced their original stance had been correct all along.

item.title: Your recall improves when you return to your original mood.
item.description: A 1981 study showed that participants remembered information better if they were in the same emotional state during retrieval as they were during encoding.

item.title: Your brain shuts down for half a second after focusing.
item.description: Participants show significantly reduced performance in detecting a second target when it appears 200 to 500 milliseconds after the first.

item.title: You hold losing investments far longer than winning ones.
item.description: A 1985 study found that investors are significantly more likely to sell a stock that has gained value than one that has dropped.

item.title: Random numbers influence your estimate of an unknown value.
item.description: A 1974 experiment demonstrated that participants' estimates for geopolitical statistics were significantly skewed by a random number drawn from a wheel of fortune.

item.title: You are statistically likely to choose the pre-selected option.
item.description: A 2003 study of organ donation found that countries with an opt-out policy had nearly 100% participation compared to 15% in opt-in countries.

item.title: You believe you understand how a simple zipper works.
item.description: A 2002 study showed that people consistently overestimate their grasp of complex systems until they are forced to explain them.

item.title: Your brain ignores most of an experience to save energy.
item.description: In a 1996 study, participants judged the total unpleasantness of a colonoscopy based heavily on the peak discomfort and the final moments of the procedure.

item.title: You assume you are safer than everyone else.
item.description: A 1980 study by Neil D. Weinstein published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology found that individuals consistently rate their own risks for negative events as lower than the risk faced by others.

item.title: You focus on one event while ignoring context.
item.description: A 2000 study showed that people overestimate the impact of a single focal event on their overall happiness.

item.title: You hold onto opinions even after being disproven.
item.description: A 1975 study showed that once an initial belief is formed, it remains influential even after the evidence supporting it is discredited.

item.title: You are a terrible judge of your future self.
item.description: A 2003 study found that people systematically underestimate how much their future preferences will change based on their current state.

item.title: You work harder as you approach a goal.
item.description: A 2006 study by Kivetz, Urminsky, and Zheng empirically resurrected the 1932 'goal-gradient hypothesis' by showing that consumers increase their purchase frequency as they approach a reward.

item.title: You feel compelled to restore your lost freedom.
item.description: Psychological reactance is a motivational state that arises when an individual's behavioral freedoms are threatened, which may lead them to resist the influence attempt to re-establish autonomy.

item.title: You overestimate how much the world focuses on you.
item.description: The spotlight effect describes your tendency to believe that your appearance and actions are more visible to others than they really are.

item.title: Your brain ignores facts that contradict your beliefs.
item.description: Motivated reasoning and biased assimilation lead people to evaluate contradictory evidence more critically than supporting evidence, causing them to perceive opposing data as less credible.

item.title: You remember events as better than they were.
item.description: The study titled 'Temporal adjustments in the evaluation of events: The rosy prospection and rosy retrospection' was published in 1997, not 1994.

item.title: The presence of others changes your moral compass.
item.description: The bystander effect demonstrates that your likelihood of intervening in an emergency decreases as the number of witnesses increases.

item.title: You change your attitude to match your behavior.
item.description: Self-perception theory suggests that when your internal beliefs are unclear, you infer them by observing your own past actions.

item.title: You create your own excuses before you even start.
item.description: Self-handicapping is the strategy of creating obstacles to performance to protect your self-esteem if you happen to fail.

item.title: Your past self is a stranger you judge harshly.
item.description: The end-of-history illusion is our tendency to believe we have reached our final personality despite significant growth over the last decade.
